sources.news_title: Trump Admin Invokes Executive Privilege in Kennedy Center Court Battle
sources.text:
The White House is arguing it has executive privilege in preventing some of President Donald Trump’s communications from being published or used in a lawsuit targeting the Kennedy Center.
In court documents filed on Wednesday, deputy counsel to the president Joshua T. Hoyt wrote in a sworn declaration that “information, documents, and communications” from the president to his advisers as well as to the Kennedy Center’s staff about its operations should be barred from release amid the ongoing litigation.
“I submit this declaration formally invoking the presidential communications privilege with respect to” those materials that were requested for discovery in the case, Hoyt also wrote.
“The communications that Plaintiff seeks are those between the President, his advisors, and/or employees of the Kennedy Center who provided advice to the President and his staff concerning the President’s duties and the effective functioning of the Kennedy Center,” Hoyt wrote in a court filing in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia.
“These communications were intended to be confidential and have remained confidential.”
Hoyt further argued that executive privilege over the president’s communications is needed in this case because, without those safeguards, Trump’s staff and advisers “would be chilled” from carrying out their duties.
His filing was issued in response to Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), a Kennedy Center board member challenging plans to shut down the Kennedy Center for renovations, and to add Trump’s name to the facility, as she seeks to obtain communications or documents related to Trump.
Earlier this month, Beatty submitted a motion to compel information from Trump because the president allegedly has refused to hand over “any documents” related to the Kennedy Center while seeking to block inquiry into those communications.
“The Department’s sweeping assertion of privilege, however, appears to be unprecedented,” her Oct. 5 filing states. “Donald Trump is the chair of a non-profit corporation’s board, and his decisions and directions lie at the heart of that board’s actions which, in turn, are the subject matter of this case.”
Also on Wednesday, the White House’s counsel wrote in a separate filing that Beatty’s demands are essentially a “fishing expedition” and argued that her attempts to produce Trump administration communications are unsubstantiated.
Beatty, they argued, could not “demonstrate that the information, documents, and communications she seeks are directly relevant to the Board’s votes to temporarily close the Center, the sole remaining issue in front of the Court,” it said.
Last month, the Kennedy Center’s board members voted to shut down the facility for two years, after a federal judge blocked a bid by Trump to return his name to the building.
Trump wrote in a Truth Social post at the time that the closure was required for safety-related repairs. The venue’s leaders have argued that the massive building, which began construction in 1965, was in dire need of renovations. A partial ceiling collapse in the building’s main hallway earlier this month intensified the calls for renovations.
U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper wrote in September that the bid to add Trump’s name to the center’s facade was illegal.
“Simply put, Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress’s blessing. The board resolution bucks a federal court order and a statute Congress enacted,” Cooper stated.

sources.text:
Donald Trump's Justice Department Seeks to Shield Private Kennedy Center Talks Amid Legal Dispute
Oct. 16 2026, Published 4:07 a.m. ET
President Donald Trump is fighting to keep his private conversations about the Kennedy Center under wraps as a bitter legal battle over the iconic performing arts venue intensifies, OK! can reveal.
According to court documents obtained by OK!, Trump's Justice Department filed a response on October 14, arguing that communications between the president, his advisers, and Kennedy Center officials must remain confidential under executive privilege.
The filing comes as Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty continues challenging plans to temporarily shutter the Washington, D.C., landmark for two years while extensive renovations take place.
Donald Trump Invokes Presidential Privilege
In the filing, government attorneys revealed that Deputy White House Counsel Joshua T. Hoyt formally invoked executive privilege at Trump's direction to prevent certain communications from being disclosed.
The administration is seeking to block Beatty's efforts to obtain documents, emails, and testimony concerning Trump's involvement in the Kennedy Center's management and operations.
The Justice Department argued that the requests threaten the constitutional separation of powers.
"Requests for discovery that pertain to the President of the United States are no ordinary matter," government lawyers declared.
Attorneys also accused Beatty of pursuing an overly broad investigation into the president's decision-making.
Donald Trump's Secret Talks Under Scrutiny
The legal fight centers on the Kennedy Center's controversial proposed two-year closure, which has already faced judicial intervention.
A federal judge previously issued a preliminary injunction blocking the board's March 16 closure decision. The administration subsequently sought to dissolve that injunction after the board reconsidered renovation plans and reviewed extensive financial and construction materials.
Court papers acknowledge that Kennedy Center official Charles Matthew Floca spoke with Trump several times in January 2026. During those conversations, Floca recommended a concentrated 24-month shutdown as the most efficient and cost-effective way to address the building's infrastructure problems.
Trump's lawyers maintain that acknowledging those discussions does not entitle Beatty to examine additional confidential presidential communications.
Want OK! each day? Sign up here!
Questions Over Donald Trump's Influence
Beatty has sought information about Trump's involvement in renovation decisions, including communications concerning the Center's finances, proposed demolition, and the timeline for closing the building.
Her discovery requests also raised questions about whether renovation funding or construction plans were connected to naming recognition for someone other than President John F. Kennedy. Government attorneys dismissed those inquiries as irrelevant to the remaining legal dispute.
They insisted the central question is whether the Kennedy Center's board fulfilled its legal responsibilities when approving the temporary shutdown.
White House Demands Secrecy
The administration maintains that the board independently reviewed substantial evidence supporting the renovations.
Trump's legal team further argued that presidential confidentiality protections extend to communications with advisers outside the White House when those discussions involve official presidential responsibilities.
The Justice Department said Beatty has already obtained thousands of pages of documents and conducted multiple depositions. Attorneys accused her of pursuing additional evidence without demonstrating sufficient legal justification.
The court has not resolved the executive privilege dispute in this filing, leaving the battle over Trump's Kennedy Center communications ongoing.

sources.news_title: Donald Trump Makes a Major Move in Kennedy Center Court Fight
sources.text:
Donald Trump just pulled a bold legal card in his fight over the Kennedy Center, and it’s raising serious questions about presidential power. The president invoked a rarely used privilege to block information requests in the ongoing court battle over the iconic venue’s future.
Donald Trump reportedly invokes executive privilege in Kennedy Center fight
President Donald Trump has formally invoked executive privilege in the legal battle over his management of the Kennedy Center, NBC News reported. White House deputy counsel Joshua Hoyt stated in a court filing that Trump directed the invocation. It covers information, documents, and communications related to the center’s management and operation.
The privilege claim responds to a lawsuit from Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex officio board member. Beatty has challenged Trump’s efforts to add his name to the building’s front. She has also contested his directive to close the center for two years of renovations.
Trump named himself to the board last year and was voted chairman by his handpicked members. He directed the center’s closure in a February social media post. He has since stated that renovations will not proceed without “recognition” for his efforts.
Beatty’s attorneys pushed back firmly against the privilege claim. “Donald Trump appointed himself as chair of the non-profit board of the Kennedy Center, and is now trying to shield his management by improperly invoking executive privilege,” lawyers Norm Eisen and Nathaniel Zelinsky said. They added that “this kind of cover-up is a direct assault on the rule of law.”
The Justice Department countered that Beatty’s document requests amounted to a “fishing expedition.” Government lawyers argued Trump’s involvement with the center “is undoubtedly in his official capacity.” Beatty’s legal team maintained that the Kennedy Center is not part of the executive branch. They argued Trump “voluntarily assumed the ‘usual powers and obligations of a trustee.’”
The center closed on Sept. 15 for emergency safety assessments and has not reopened. Federal Judge Christopher Cooper has not yet ruled on the privilege dispute.

sources.news_title: What is executive privilege? Trump's move in Kennedy Center case explained
sources.text:
What is executive privilege? Trump's move in Kennedy Center case explained
Trump invoked executive privilege to withhold Kennedy Center records as Rep. Joyce Beatty challenges plans to close the venue for renovations.
President Donald Trump has invoked executive privilege to keep certain records about the Kennedy Center from being shared with Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty of Ohio. The move comes as Beatty challenges Trump’s plans to close the performing arts venue for two years for renovations.
In a court filing on Wednesday, October 14, White House deputy counsel Joshua Hoyt told a federal judge that the protection covers communications between Trump, his advisers and Kennedy Center employees.
The records concern the president’s role in the institution and its management. The dispute raises questions about whether Trump can use executive privilege to protect communications linked to his separate role as chairman of the Kennedy Center’s board.
What is executive privilege?
Executive privilege is the president’s ability to keep certain government communications confidential, particularly discussions with advisers about official decisions. It is meant to allow the president and those working with him to discuss options and give advice without fearing that every conversation will become public.
However, this protection is not unlimited. Courts can require the release of protected information if the need for it is strong enough. The Congressional Research Service has explained that presidential communications privilege is qualified, meaning it can be overcome when there is an adequate need for the records.
Why has Trump invoked executive privilege?
Hoyt argued that Trump needs access to information about the Kennedy Center because the president appoints members of its board and the Advisory Committee on the Arts. This, he said, requires Trump to understand the institution’s management, operations, fundraising and planned activities.
"I believe that, without the protection of the presidential communications privilege over the communications described above, presidential advisors and their staff members would be chilled from gathering relevant information, exploring alternatives, and providing fully informed recommendations regarding the performance of the President's duties," Hoyt wrote in his declaration.
In a separate court filing, Justice Department lawyers accused Beatty of conducting a "fishing expedition" and argued that her requests raised concerns about the separation of powers.
Beatty’s lawyers, however, say the government is using privilege too broadly to prevent her from obtaining records about Trump’s involvement in decisions affecting the Kennedy Center.
How is the Kennedy Center lawsuit linked to Trump?
Beatty filed her lawsuit in December, challenging the board’s decision to add Trump’s name to the Kennedy Center and plans to close the building for two years for renovations. She is also an ex officio member of the board of trustees.
Trump became the board’s chairman last year, making him the first sitting president to hold the position. The center, established by Congress in 1958, receives federal funding as well as money from ticket sales and private donations.
The dispute also covers the center’s financial condition, plans to change its name and discussions about whether the building could be demolished. Trump previously said the venue could be "ripped down" if he and his administration did not receive recognition for their work on repairs and fundraising.
Judge blocks Trump’s Kennedy Center closure
In May, US District Judge Christopher Cooper blocked the planned closure and ordered Trump’s name removed from the building’s facade. Workers removed the name in June.
The judge also allowed Beatty to seek records and question officials about the closure plans and possible demolition. Her legal team says the Justice Department has since blocked questions about instructions Trump gave Kennedy Center staff and withheld related documents.
During a deposition last week, a Justice Department lawyer repeatedly told Matthew Floca, the center’s executive director and chief operating officer, not to answer certain questions, citing executive privilege.
The judge will now have to address the dispute over which records can remain protected and which must be provided to Beatty’s legal team.

sources.news_title: Trump invokes executive privilege in Kennedy Center court fight
sources.text:
A White House lawyer said President Donald Trump has officially invoked executive privilege in the court fight involving his management of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.
In a court filing late Wednesday, Joshua Hoyt, a deputy assistant and deputy counsel to the president, said that at “the direction of the President,” he was “formally invoking the presidential communications privilege with respect to information, documents, and communications requested” by the plaintiff in the case, Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio.
Beatty, an ex officio board member of the center, has been challenging Trump’s efforts to add his name to the front of the building and his directive that the center be shuttered for two years while it’s renovated.
She’s been seeking more information about Trump’s role in both matters, since he named himself to the board last year and was voted chairman by his handpicked board members. In February, Trump directed the center to be closed for renovations in a social media post and has since said those renovations won’t proceed if he doesn’t get “recognition” for his efforts.
Beatty contends the board’s subsequent votes to close the center were a fait accompli, given Trump’s February directive.
In the administration’s court filing Wednesday, Hoyt said the executive privilege invocation means Beatty is not entitled to any more details about the president’s management of the nonprofit board.
He said in a declaration that privilege specifically covers “information, documents, and communications shared between the President, his advisors (government and non-government), and Kennedy Center staff, pertaining to the management and operation” of the center. It also extends to communications “to or from his advisors and/or Kennedy Center staff.”
In a separate filing Wednesday, the Justice Department said Beatty was engaged in an improper “fishing expedition,” arguing her “pursuit of irrelevant evidence does not justify her extraordinary request” for additional documents and information.
Beatty’s attorneys asserted it was the DOJ that was acting in extraordinary fashion.
“Donald Trump appointed himself as chair of the non-profit board of the Kennedy Center, and is now trying to shield his management by improperly invoking executive privilege,” the lawyers, Norm Eisen of Democracy Defenders Action and Nathaniel Zelinsky of Washington Litigation Group, said in a statement.
“The Supreme Court has stressed that the government should not invoke executive privilege lightly, but that is precisely what the Department of Justice is doing here. This kind of cover-up is a direct assault on the rule of law,” they said.
Lawyers for the DOJ had said in a filing earlier this month that Trump would be claiming executive privilege, but he did not formally do so until Wednesday.
In an Oct. 6 filing, Beatty’s attorneys said there were no grounds to claim the privilege, since Trump is a defendant in the case as chairman of the congressionally created center’s board, and not as president.

The attorneys said the Kennedy Center is not part of the executive branch “and does not exercise executive power.” They added that Trump “voluntarily assumed the ‘usual powers and obligations of a trustee.’”
“Trustee and board chair are not roles that must be performed by the President of the United States and, indeed, never have been in the Center’s history before now. Nor are the staff at the Kennedy Center anything like the close presidential advisers whose conversations executive privilege protects,” the lawyers argued. “The Court should not permit Defendants to evade accountability as trustees by abusing a privilege constructed for other purposes, not the chairmanship of this non-profit entity.”
“Allowing Defendants to hide behind this unwarranted assertion of privilege would obstruct the search for the truth” and “undermine public confidence in these important proceedings,” they added.
The Justice Department countered that Trump’s involvement with the center “is undoubtedly in his official capacity,” since it’s the president’s duty to appoint board members.
And, the government lawyers said, the president is always the president.
Beatty “argues that executive privilege ‘protects the institution of the Presidency, not the individual who happens to occupy the White House.’ But, as the Supreme Court reinforced recently, the Framers vested ‘the executive Power’ in one person—‘a President of the United States of America.’”
The federal judge presiding over the case, Christopher Cooper, has not yet weighed in on the issue, but the administration’s stance conflicts with a ruling he issued this month allowing Beatty’s team to learn more about the circumstances surrounding a photo of Trump on Air Force One viewing a poster that read “Kennedy Center DEMOLISH.”

President Donald Trump invoked his executive privilege in the lawsuit his administration is facing over the Kennedy Center from Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-OH).
White House associate counsel Josh Hoyt wrote in a court declaration on Thursday that Trump was declaring his presidential communications privilege for communications, information, and documents requested by Beatty and her lawyers in the lawsuit. This would shield information that Beatty requests from becoming public and shared with her based on the separation of powers.

Hoyt says the privilege applies to “information, documents, and communications shared between the President, his advisors (government and non-government), and Kennedy Center staff, pertaining to the management and operation of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.” He also clarified that it includes communications between his advisers and Kennedy Center staff related to his decision-making on the facility.
The Department of Justice lawyers filed Hoyt’s declaration alongside a response from the Trump administration asking the court to deny a motion from Beatty to compel information related to the White House’s communications with the Kennedy Center. The lawyers wrote that Beatty’s motion to compel is a “fishing expedition” that poses “obvious separation-of-powers concerns.”
Beatty’s lawyers filed the motion to compel after lawyers for Kennedy Center Executive Director Matt Floca invoked the presidential communications privilege during Floca’s testimony. The executive privilege came in response to questions about Floca’s conversations with Trump and executive branch officials, according to court filings.
Now that the Trump administration has invoked the presidential communications privilege, the court can either grant Beatty’s motion to compel and reject the administration’s use of executive privilege or side with the administration’s argument and allow the use of executive privilege in this case, which would block the communications from Beatty.
The back-and-forth is the latest development in the legal saga between the Trump administration and Beatty, an ex officio member of the board, over Trump’s planned construction of the Kennedy Center. Beatty sued the administration over its plans to close the facility for a two-year renovation and its intention to rename the facility after Trump.
The main building of the performing arts center is temporarily closed as the facility examines whether it is safe to reopen to the public in its current condition. The name-change effort has been stalled, as the administration and Kennedy Center board argue Trump should be recognized on the facade for his contributions to the facility and its planned reconstruction, but that it should not be renamed entirely.

Trump's lawyers are now drawing from that same precedent to argue Trump should not be forced to disclose information about his efforts to rename the Kennedy Center.
"The DOJ, in response to Kennedy Center board of trustees member Rep. Joyce Beatty's motion to compel discovery, told U.S. District Judge Christopher 'Casey' Cooper on Wednesday that the Democratic lawmaker's requests should fail across the board," reported Law and Crime's Matt Naham on Thursday."The DOJ first mentioned Cheney v. United States in the opening paragraph of the filing."
In the filing, the Trump administration argued that "requests for discovery that pertain to the President of the United States are no ordinary matter. Instead, they raise distinct separation-of-powers concerns. Both the Supreme Court and the D.C. Circuit have recognized as much time and again," the filing said. "Thus, a plaintiff may not serve overbroad discovery requests on the President and expect a line-by-line response. See Cheney v. U.S. Dist. Ct. for D.C., 542 U.S. 367, 388 (2004)."
This is not the first time that Cheney's legacy of expanding the power of the executive branch has helped Trump implement his own agenda.
In a 2025 op-ed for the New York Times, Ron Suskind argued that "[Cheney] wrote a playbook of how to exercise executive authority beyond constitutional boundaries and the rule of law. Donald Trump has added pages and is working on a sequel."
From invading Iraq despite questionable evidence, establishing mass surveillance throughout the United States and declaring emergencies to achieve his goals through executive orders, Cheney made it possible for the executive branch to act on its own authority in ways not seen before.
"Disastrous as those all actions were, Mr. Trump has undertaken even more significant expansions of power and illegality, often under even more dubious claims of emergency," Suskind observed. "... Mr. Cheney made it possible."

sources.news_title: Trump Invokes Executive Privilege in Kennedy Center Closure Fight
sources.text:
Washington — President Trump has formally asserted executive privilege over records sought by Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty of Ohio in her continuing legal challenge to his attempt to temporarily close the Kennedy Center for renovations.
White House Deputy Counsel Joshua Hoyt notified a federal judge Wednesday that Mr. Trump was invoking the presidential communications privilege, a category of executive privilege. Hoyt said the assertion applies to information, documents and communications involving Mr. Trump, his advisers and Kennedy Center employees concerning the president’s responsibilities and “the effective functioning” of the performing arts institution.
Hoyt maintained that Mr. Trump needs to “familiarize himself” with the center’s management, operations, fundraising and programming because the president appoints members of its board and the related Advisory Committee on the Arts.
“I believe that, without the protection of the presidential communications privilege over the communications described above, presidential advisors and their staff members would be chilled from gathering relevant information, exploring alternatives, and providing fully informed recommendations regarding the performance of the President’s duties,” the White House lawyer wrote in a declaration.
In a separate court filing, Justice Department attorneys accused Beatty of pursuing a “fishing expedition” that, they said, could raise separation-of-powers issues.
“Even though the President’s statutory duties and the Chairman’s trust duties overlap, what matters for the purpose of executive privilege is that Plaintiff seeks information, documents, and communications concerning the President’s actions in his official capacity,” the lawyers wrote.
Executive privilege is not unlimited. Courts may set it aside when a party makes a sufficient showing that the requested information is necessary.
The Kennedy Center’s board of trustees, which includes Trump administration officials and presidential allies, elected Mr. Trump as its chairman last year. He became the first sitting president to hold that position. His effort to use executive privilege to withhold Kennedy Center records presents new and unresolved questions about whether the protection covers actions he took as chairman of the performing arts institution, which Congress created in 1958 and which relies on federal funding, ticket sales and private donations.
The president’s privilege claim covers records concerning his plan to close the Kennedy Center for two years for renovations, the institution’s finances, an effort to place Mr. Trump’s name on the building’s facade and the possibility of demolishing the center.
Questions about a potential demolition intensified after Mr. Trump said last month that the Kennedy Center would close and “end up being ripped down” unless he and his administration received credit for fundraising and leading repairs at the institution.
Mr. Trump was also photographed aboard Air Force One examining a placard that appeared to read “Kennedy Center Demolished.”
The dispute over executive privilege is unfolding in a lawsuit Beatty filed in December. The case challenges the board’s decision to rename the center the Donald J. Trump and The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts and to close it for two years of renovations. Beatty serves as an ex officio member of the Kennedy Center’s Board of Trustees.
In May, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper halted the planned closure and directed that Mr. Trump’s name be removed from the building’s facade. Workers removed the president’s name from the exterior in June, although a tarp now covers the front portico and obscures much of the building’s name.
Cooper has also authorized Beatty to obtain information from the Kennedy Center about the decision to close its main building and any possible demolition. He also permitted her to conduct depositions as part of the discovery process.
Beatty’s attorneys, however, said the Justice Department was attempting to stop her from asking about instructions or other input Kennedy Center employees received from Mr. Trump as board chairman. They also said the department had refused to produce documents concerning those communications.
The lawyers accused the department of “improperly asserting a blanket privilege in an unprecedented fashion” and asked Cooper to order the Kennedy Center to provide the records Beatty is seeking.
In a response to Beatty’s requests, Justice Department attorneys argued late last month that “to the extent the discovery requests seek communications involving the President or White House personnel, they are inappropriate because they may have the effect of seeking information protected by the presidential communications privilege.”
During a deposition last week, Matthew Floca, the Kennedy Center’s executive director and chief operating officer, was repeatedly told by a Justice Department lawyer not to answer certain questions from one of Beatty’s attorneys because of the government’s protective assertion of executive privilege.

sources.news_title: Trump deploys 'nuclear option' to shield himself amid 'missing' Kennedy Center funds
sources.text:
Traffic moves along Rock Creek Parkway near the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C., US, October 5, 2026. This year's Kennedy Center Honors will be held at Washington's Capital One Arena as the Trump administration faces legal and congressional challenges over plans to demolish the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, a center spokesperson said on Friday. REUTERS/Eric Lee
President Donald Trump invoked executive privilege to shield his Kennedy Center records as the White House examines claims that a multimillion-dollar donation went missing.
White House deputy counsel Joshua Hoyt formally asserted the privilege in a declaration filed Wednesday in a federal lawsuit brought by Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-OH) over the crusade to include Trump's name on the building.
Hoyt’s claim covers the fundraising efforts of the board that runs the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, even as the White House reviews an alleged donation that never reached the center, Axios reported.
In a headline, The New Republic called the move Trump’s “nuclear option” to hide records from a judge.
The withheld records cover Trump’s push to close the center, its finances, the effort to put his name on the building and whether it could be demolished.
Trump has moved to invoke privilege for communications with his advisers and Kennedy Center staff about the center’s “management and operation,” Hoyt wrote. Trump also wants to extend it to advisers outside the government and even to talks that did not include the president.
The claim also blocks answers to certain questions asked in depositions, or sworn interviews, of Kennedy Center Executive Director Matthew Floca and another witness, the declaration says. That includes communications involving Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick that “relayed presidential decision-making.”
Hoyt wrote that the claim rests on Trump’s power to appoint the center’s trustees and members of its Advisory Committee on the Arts, which helps the board raise money.
“The President must familiarize himself with current and planned cultural activities, along with the Board’s fundraising efforts, to ensure that the committee members he designates are well-suited to meeting the challenges facing the Kennedy Center,” he wrote.
“The President’s communications in furtherance of these duties overlap with the President’s duties as Chairman of the Board,” Hoyt wrote, adding that staffers would be "chilled" if the privilege was not invoked.
Taken together, the passages stretch a shield built for candid presidential advice to cover arts center management. Trump is the first sitting president to chair the center’s board, which elected him last year.
Beatty, who sits on the center’s board, sued in December to block the board’s push to rename the center for Trump and close it. Her lawyers have accused the Justice Department of “improperly asserting a blanket privilege in an unprecedented fashion."
Justice Department lawyers accused Beatty of a “fishing expedition” in a separate filing.
Trump directed his White House counsel to look into the donation claim, which former U.S. Attorney Alina Habba raised in the Oval Office last Friday, according to Axios. She told Trump that former Kennedy Center President Ric Grenell failed to deposit a donation her billionaire husband, Turhan Mildon, made a year ago.
“Absurd. I’ve never asked for one cent to be sent somewhere else pretending it was for the Kennedy Center, and I’ve never received any payment from him at all,” Grenell said in a statement to Axios.
Kennedy Center staff searched late last year for a contribution they thought was $6 million but couldn't find it, an official told Axios. The center’s records showed Mildon owed only a $270,000 pledge, which he paid Tuesday.
The center’s finances have collapsed since Trump took control, The Washington Post reported last month, finding it borrowed everything its bank would lend and wrote off pledges from donors who stopped paying.
“POTUS doesn’t want to deal with this. Of course, he’s concerned. But if there is missing money, this is a big, big problem,” another administration official told Axios.

sources.news_title: Trump Administration Formally Invokes Executive Privilege in Kennedy Center Lawsuit
sources.text:
The Trump administration has formally invoked presidential communications privilege to withhold documents and block testimony about the president’s involvement in the Kennedy Center’s management, escalating a legal fight over the performing arts institution’s planned two-year closure.
The court filing Wednesday by Deputy White House Counsel Joshua Hoyt asserted the privilege covered communications between Trump, his advisers and Kennedy Center staff about the institution’s management and operations.
The declaration specifically identifies requests for documents, written answers and deposition testimony that the administration says could reveal presidential decision-making. It also covers some communications involving Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has been involved in discussions related to the Kennedy Center.
The filing comes after Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex officio member of the Kennedy Center’s board, challenged the administration’s earlier objections to producing evidence in the case.
Trending
Beatty is seeking information as she fights the board’s decision to close the center’s main building for two years to conduct renovations. She has argued that the discovery is necessary to understand the board’s decision-making and whether it fulfilled its legal obligations.
The administration, in its response last week to Beatty’s motion to compel, urged U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper to reject her request, arguing that she has already received more than enough evidence to challenge the closure.
“The record as it stands” provides enough evidence for the court to uphold the board’s decision and grant summary judgment to the administration, the Wednesday filing said.
The dispute over privilege has surfaced during depositions, including the questioning of Matt Floca, the executive director for the Kennedy Center, who testified on the institution’s behalf on Oct. 7.
During that deposition, Beatty’s attorney questioned Floca about Trump’s public statements tying the planned renovation to the outcome of a separate legal fight over the center’s renaming.
Trump wrote on Truth Social on Sept. 15 that the renovation and reconstruction would not take place if the D.C. Circuit ruled against the board’s approved name change and the decision was not overturned by the Supreme Court.
Asked whether anyone at the center had discussed Trump’s statement with him, Floca’s attorney objected on executive privilege grounds and instructed him not to answer.
Floca had testified that the center takes direction through board resolutions or committee guidance. Asked whether Trump could direct management to delay renovations without board approval, Floca said the center responds to the board and that such an instruction would need to be formalized through a resolution.
“I don’t know what to expect,” Floca said when asked whether the center anticipated Trump might direct or suggest that renovations should not proceed until he received the recognition he sought.
The administration’s declaration seeks to protect communications that could explain how Trump’s public statements intersected with private discussions among his advisers and Kennedy Center staff.
Hoyt argued that the president’s role in appointing the center’s trustees and members of its Advisory Committee on the Arts required him to remain informed about the institution’s management, operations and performance. He said the communications at issue were intended to remain confidential and that disclosure could discourage advisers from providing candid recommendations.
Beatty’s legal team has challenged whether executive privilege can be used so broadly in a dispute concerning the Kennedy Center board’s responsibilities. The administration countered that the president’s official duties extend to statutory responsibilities involving the center and that the privilege can cover communications with advisers outside the White House, including private advisers.
The administration also argued that Beatty has not demonstrated a sufficient need for the protected material. The remaining issue in the case, it said, is whether the board had sufficient basis to vote to temporarily close the center for repairs and renovations — a question that could be answered using the materials presented to the board before its votes.
The filing said Beatty has already received more than 7,500 pages of documents, participated in five depositions and obtained responses to 44 requests for admission.
Cooper previously blocked the board’s initial plan to close the Kennedy Center. Since then, both sides have quickly gathered evidence as the administration asks the judge to lift the preliminary injunction and rule in its favor without a trial.

sources.news_title: Trump Uses Nuclear Option to Hide Kennedy Center Docs From Judge
sources.text:
Trump Uses Nuclear Option to Keep Kennedy Center Documents Hidden
Donald Trump wants to hide the true extent of his Kennedy Center takeover.
The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C., on October 1
SAUL LOEB/AFP/Getty Images
The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C., on October 1
President Trump is fighting attempts to make him testify and produce documents related to his takeover of the Kennedy Center.
In a court filing Wednesday, Trump asserted executive privilege, claiming that in her lawsuit, Kennedy Center board member and Democratic Representative Joyce Beatty initiated “overbroad discovery requests that expressly implicated the President’s involvement in the Kennedy Center’s management and operations, and called for information, documents, and communications concerning that involvement.”
“Those requests are improper, and this Court should deny Plaintiff’s motion to compel. Plaintiff’s arguments to the contrary fail to convince,” the president’s deputy assistant and deputy counsel, Joshua Hoyt, wrote in the document.
Beatty sued Trump late last year over his attempts to take over the center, add his name, and shut it down for repairs. Since then, the president has pressed on with his handpicked board of trustees, rebranding the center with his name and closing it so it can be renovated to his liking, defying multiple court orders along the way.
Now Trump is refusing to testify or provide documentation about his involvement, asserting executive privilege over a pet project that shouldn’t be anywhere near his top priorities as president. His takeover has not so coincidentally coincided with the center’s financial collapse, with most of its cash reserves gone. Donations and pledges are drying up, and ticket sales have plummeted.
“The burst happened up the pipe,” said Andrew Taylor, director of the arts management program at American University, to The Washington Post last month. “The water stopped flowing into the organization because of the choices the administration was making.”
Trump claims that only his name and takeover can save the center from physical and financial ruin. But it seems that things have only gotten worse since he got involved, much like everything else in the U.S.
Trump Says He’d Let MAGA Fan Who “Looks Like Shit” Die at His Rally
Donald Trump went on to refer to people who get sick at his rallies as “collateral damage.”
President Donald Trump at a campaign rally in Kalispell, Montana, on October 14
Kent NISHIMURA/AFP/Getty Images
President Donald Trump at a campaign rally in Kalispell, Montana, on October 14
President Trump would let his friend who “looks like shit” die at his rally.
“I travel with more doctors than any human being. If people get sick in the audience, they leave ’em alone. You know what they call them? Collateral damage,” Trump said at his Wednesday rally in Arizona, receiving some chuckles from the crowd. “If that person right over there, a friend of mine—he looks like shit, actually. He looks like he’s ready to have a heart attack. If he actually had a heart attack, you know what my doctors would do? … They would leave him alone!”
Trump: I travel with doctors. If people get sick in the audience, they leave them alone. You know what they call them? Collateral damage. If that person right over there, he looks like shit actually. He looks like he's ready to have a heart attack. If he did, my doctors would leave him alone.
“I say, ‘Please help him!’ They’d say, ‘No sir, we can’t leave your side.’ But he’s dying of a heart attack! ‘Sir, he’s collateral damage,’” he continued. “Can you believe it? They got like six ambulances, and they won’t use one for anybody else.”
It’s unclear who exactly Trump was saying “looks like shit.” But the crowd full of his most loyal supporters just laughed along with him—as if they weren’t collateral damage to him too.
Some commentators pointed to Trump’s lack of filter as a sign of dementia, and indeed shortly before his remarks, Trump was bragging about acing a dementia test.
CNN medical analyst Jonathan Reiner challenged Trump’s notion that doctors would ignore sick people or refer to them as collateral damage.
“This is completely untrue, and an actual insult to the fabulous doctors, nurses, and PAs of the White House Medical Unit,” he wrote online. “Over the years I’ve been honored to get to know many members of the WHMU and I know that they would never call a spectator ‘collateral damage’. They would save their life.”
Trump is determined to punish the Democratic representative just for being an immigrant.
Representative Ilhan Omar
Stephen Maturen/Getty Images
Representative Ilhan Omar
President Donald Trump wants to build a case to strip Representative Ilhan Omar of her citizenship and deport her.
The Wall Street Journalreported Wednesday that the federal government is investigating how Omar got her citizenship after she arrived in the U.S. from Somalia as a child, focusing on how her late father filled out her forms. Her Washington, D.C., home was searched on Monday, just three weeks before the midterm elections in November.
Homeland Security agents took her cellphone, notebooks, personal computers, and passport. Several subpoenas have been issued to her relatives and others close to her. It’s obvious that the Trump administration wants to make an example out of her as part of its effort to begin denaturalizing American citizens.
The investigation ostensibly centers on whether Omar’s father put her age as 17 rather than 18 on her citizenship application to allow her to qualify immediately for citizenship alongside his own application. Omar became a citizen in 2000.
“They cheat on everything,” Trump said to an Ohio audience at a rally Monday about Somali Americans. “We’re not going to stand for it.”
In order to strip an American of their citizenship, the Department of Justice has to sue in federal court and prove that the person materially lied to get their status. For years, conservatives have pushed the unfounded rumor that Omar married her brother to bring him to the U.S. Investigations by media outlets and the government have yielded nothing incriminating about her.
Trump’s effort is a racist attempt to single out a Black, hijab-wearing Muslim of Somali descent to satisfy his and the Republican Party’s bigotry. The case is an uphill battle and will result in a drawn-out court fight, but they want to be as cruel and inflict as much damage on Omar and her reputation as possible.
Elon Musk Throws Trump Under the Bus for Ukraine Intel Disruption
The tech billionaire said that systems that went offline during a Russian missile attack that killed nine are “owned and controlled” by the U.S. military and “ultimately POTUS.”
Elon Musk and Donald Trump in 2024
Kayla Bartkowski/Getty Images
Elon Musk and Donald Trump in 2024
Elon Musk is wiping his hands of the Trump administration’s latest intel scandal.
The SpaceX founder did not deny that his company’s satellite-supplied internet service was suspended in Ukraine earlier this week as Russian missiles barraged Kyiv. Instead, he blamed the lapse on the U.S. military and Donald Trump.
In a statement on X, Musk wrote that “Starshield systems are owned and controlled” by Washington and “any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.”
“Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX,” Musk continued. “Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”
But Ukraine’s actions on Tuesday were not offensive. Russian ballistic missiles slammed two plants supplying heat and electricity to Kyiv and damaged a residential building in the capital. At least nine people died in the attacks, reported Al Jazeera.
Ukrainian officials suggested that the strikes could have been prevented if they received the proper intelligence—but there was only radio silence. Multiple sources familiar with the matter told CBS News that U.S. officials had claimed their defense systems had failed to detect the missiles because of “bad weather,” but Kyiv did not buy the excuse.
Around the same time, SpaceX restricted Starlink access within the region, upending Ukraine’s primary internet connection.
On Friday, Trump brokered an eyebrow-raising deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from Moscow, effectively offering the country an economic lifeline that would allow Russia to continue the war.
Zelenskiy torched the deal, arguing to American officials that the arrangement exhibited “weakness.” Trump, apparently, did not appreciate the language choice.
A multiday harassment campaign ensued, in which the Trump administration called European capitals and Kyiv, threatening to cut off military intelligence sharing and weapons deliveries unless Ukraine stopped attacking Russian oil refineries.
On Wednesday, Zelenskiy told Piers Morgan that he felt “betrayed” by Trump and the U.S.
“This is our country, our body, our home, our children.… That’s why it’s painful when Trump chooses one side,” the Ukrainian president said in a clip of the interview shared on X.
“If you’re in the middle, you have to stay in the middle. Not on the wrong side,” continued Zelenskiy. “This is not the right side of history.”
DOJ Begs Judge to Ignore Hegseth as She Considers Making Him Testify
A federal judge wants Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to explain all his anti-trans posts on social media. The Justice Department is asking her to pretend the posts don’t exist.
Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
A federal judge is considering forcing Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth to testify in court about his anti-transgender statements for a lawsuit challenging the U.S. military’s ban on transgender people.
U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes said in court in Washington, D.C., Wednesday that she might compel Hegseth to sit for a one-hour deposition and answer questions about the anti-trans views he has expressed.
“I’m very aware that he is the secretary of defense and he has a lot of constraints on his time. But he has time to tweet and put out videos and speak to generals, and I think it’s fair game,” Reyes said, according to The Washington Sun’s Jose Pagliery.
First, though, Reyes said she’d give Hegseth the chance to respond to 10 written questions, and if he isn’t forthcoming enough and is too “lawyerly,” then he’d have to sit for the deposition.
The Department of Justice’s lawyers, meanwhile, don’t want Reyes to take Hegseth’s past statements or social media posts into consideration.
“The Supreme Court has held that courts should not look outside the operative terms of a policy—as this Court did with respect to certain social media posts—in assessing the basis on which a policy classifies,” the DOJ wrote in a four-page court filing Tuesday seeking summary judgment in favor of the government from Reyes.
Hegseth has a long history of making anti-trans comments—both in public and on social media.
On February 27, 2025, Hegseth shared an official Department of War post stating, “Transgender service members are disqualified from service without an exemption.” On April 20 the same year, he posted, “Your agenda is illegals, trans & DEI—all of which are no longer allowed @ DoD.” On April 24, he called Reyes “a rogue judge” and claimed there were “Zero readiness reasons for trans troops.”
In a speech on May 6, Hegseth declared, “No more dudes in dresses, we’re done with that shit.” And after the Supreme Court later allowed the ban to remain in place while the legal battle continued, Hegseth posted on May 8, “After a SCOTUS victory for @POTUS, TRANS is out at the DOD.”
In Reyes’s March 2025 ruling temporarily halting the military’s ban, well before these posts, she said the military’s policy was “soaked in animus and dripping with pretext.” That proved prescient, as in June this year, the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled against the ban in a 2–1 decision.
The Pentagon is trying to delay enforcement of that decision, pending an appeal to the Supreme Court, while the lawsuit’s plaintiffs, service members who are already being pushed out, want the appeals court to mandate compliance immediately.

sources.news_title: EXECUTIVE PRIVILEGE SHOWDOWN: Trump Refuses to Release White House Communications in Kennedy Center Legal Battle
sources.text:
President Donald Trump has formally asserted executive privilege in a federal court dispute over his leadership of the Kennedy Center, seeking to prevent the disclosure of internal communications concerning his management of the Washington performing arts institution, including controversial plans to rename the facility and shut it down for extensive renovations.
The administration’s latest legal maneuver comes as Rep. Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat who serves on the Kennedy Center’s board by virtue of her congressional position, challenges the president’s authority to make major decisions affecting the institution. At the heart of the case is whether Trump can claim the confidentiality protections afforded to presidential communications while acting as chairman of the Kennedy Center’s nonprofit governing board.
In documents submitted to the court Wednesday night, Joshua Hoyt, a deputy assistant and deputy counsel to the president, stated that he was acting at “the direction of the President” in invoking executive privilege over records and correspondence requested by Beatty. The filing was reported Thursday by NBC News.
Trump assumed control of the Kennedy Center’s board last year after appointing new members, who subsequently selected him to serve as chairman. His leadership has generated legal challenges over proposed changes to the institution, including efforts to place his name on the building and a sweeping renovation project that would keep the center closed for two years.
The president publicly announced the planned shutdown in February through a social media post. He subsequently indicated that the renovation initiative would not move forward without receiving “recognition” for his involvement.
Beatty’s lawsuit maintains that Trump’s public declaration effectively predetermined the center’s closure, leaving the board to formally approve a decision that had already been made. Her attorneys have sought internal communications to determine how the decision was reached and whether the board exercised independent authority.
The White House has resisted those demands, arguing that discussions involving the president and individuals advising him on Kennedy Center matters fall within the scope of executive privilege.
In his declaration, Hoyt described the protected material as “information, documents, and communications shared between the President, his advisors (government and non-government), and Kennedy Center staff, pertaining to the management and operation” of the institution. He also asserted confidentiality protections for communications “to or from his advisors and/or Kennedy Center staff.”
Justice Department attorneys reinforced the administration’s position in a separate submission Wednesday, accusing Beatty of pursuing an unjustified “fishing expedition” through presidential records.
The department argued that her “pursuit of irrelevant evidence does not justify her extraordinary request” for further documentation.
Beatty’s legal representatives, Norm Eisen of Democracy Defenders Action and Nathaniel Zelinsky of Washington Litigation Group, responded by accusing the president of attempting to use his constitutional office to conceal decisions made in his separate role overseeing a nonprofit organization.
“Donald Trump appointed himself as chair of the non-profit board of the Kennedy Center, and is now trying to shield his management by improperly invoking executive privilege,” they said in a statement.
“The Supreme Court has stressed that the government should not invoke executive privilege lightly, but that is precisely what the Department of Justice is doing here. This kind of cover-up is a direct assault on the rule of law,” they said.
The administration had already signaled earlier in October that Trump intended to rely on executive privilege. Wednesday’s submission, however, marked the formal assertion of that protection in the ongoing litigation.
In an October 6 court filing, Beatty’s lawyers argued that the president’s participation in the Kennedy Center’s governance must be distinguished from his constitutional responsibilities as chief executive. They maintained that the institution, although established by Congress, operates independently of the executive branch “and does not exercise executive power.”
“Trustee and board chair are not roles that must be performed by the President of the United States and, indeed, never have been in the Center’s history before now,” the attorneys wrote.
Federal government lawyers rejected that distinction, maintaining that Trump’s oversight of the Kennedy Center “is undoubtedly in his official capacity,” particularly because federal law gives the president authority to appoint members of the institution’s governing board.
The disagreement raises a potentially significant legal question about the boundaries of presidential confidentiality protections when a sitting president simultaneously exercises authority over an organization outside the traditional federal executive structure.
U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper, who is presiding over the lawsuit, has yet to determine whether the disputed communications are protected from disclosure.
Earlier this month, Cooper authorized Beatty’s legal team to pursue information relating to a photograph of Trump aboard Air Force One reviewing a poster displaying the words “Kennedy Center DEMOLISH.” The image has become another point of contention as the parties dispute the administration’s plans for the facility.
The Kennedy Center itself has already suspended operations. Officials closed the venue on September 15, citing the need for emergency safety evaluations, and it has remained shuttered since then.
The dispute also follows earlier court intervention in Trump’s plans for the institution. In May, Judge Cooper blocked a previous closure decision and ordered the removal of Trump’s name from the building’s facade. The ruling did not prohibit necessary repairs or prevent the board from considering a new shutdown through an independent decision-making process.
The renovation project has been described as a roughly $257 million undertaking, with administration officials maintaining that major improvements are necessary to address the building’s condition. Trump and his allies have argued that closing the center would allow the work to proceed more efficiently and help restore the venue to a higher standard.
The legal controversy intensified in September when the Kennedy Center’s board voted to close the institution immediately, prompting further objections from Beatty and renewed scrutiny of whether the shutdown complied with the court’s earlier restrictions.
Another issue concerns the administration’s refusal to permit certain questions during depositions. Justice Department attorneys previously instructed Kennedy Center officials not to disclose communications involving Trump, citing presidential confidentiality protections even before the privilege was formally asserted.
Judge Cooper must now decide whether the administration’s claim is legally justified and whether Beatty can obtain the information she says is necessary to challenge the president’s decisions.
Meanwhile, the Kennedy Center remains closed, with its future operations and renovation plans still entangled in the federal court battle.

sources.news_title: Executive Privilege: US Department Of Justice Invokes Presidential Protection To Shield Trump’s Role In Kennedy Center Legal Battle
Trump Invokes Cheney Precedent to Shield Kennedy Center Input
sources.text:
President Donald Trump once called Dick Cheney “irrelevant” and said he was “never a fan.” Now, however, Trump is relying on a legal precedent involving the late former vice president to keep details of his “deliberations” about the Kennedy Center’s future from being disclosed in discovery.
The Justice Department made that argument Wednesday in opposing a motion to compel discovery filed by Kennedy Center board of trustees member Rep. Joyce Beatty. In a filing to U.S. District Judge Christopher “Casey” Cooper, the DOJ argued that Beatty’s requests should be rejected in their entirety.
The government invoked Cheney v. United States in the opening paragraph of its response.

The DOJ also argued that Trump’s simultaneous role as the Kennedy Center board’s chairman “is of no moment.” It said Beatty’s “extraordinarily weak justification for an extraordinarily intrusive discovery campaign” fails regardless of that dual role.
“In other words, even though the President’s statutory duties and the Chairman’s trust duties overlap, what matters for the purpose of executive privilege is that Plaintiff seeks information, documents, and communications concerning the President’s actions in his official capacity,” the filing stated. The government acknowledged that Trump “has at various times participated in renovation planning at the Center.”
The government rejected Beatty’s argument that the case differs from Cheney. “For three reasons, Plaintiff asserts that ‘[t]his Is Not A Cheney Case.’ All three are wrong,” the filing said. It also disputed claims that the administration had stonewalled Beatty, saying it had produced “more than 7,500 pages” of “documents and responses.”
